name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Friday 8 January 1982

clue.text: The Mad Hatter's a menace

indicators.note: something mad is deranged, its parts thrown out of their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written; the Mad Hatter is the Alice in Wonderland character

explanation.surface: Lewis Carroll's Mad Hatter is described as a danger to those around him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad Hatter' reads as one famous name, but 'Mad' is split off to work on the six letters of the other word.
explanation.definitionFit: A threat is something or someone likely to cause harm, which is what a menace is.

clue.text: Lock-keepers play musical skittles?

blocks.note: Hair is the 1960s rock musical
skittles are the pins knocked down in bowling

explanation.surface: Canal lock-keepers pass the time with a musical version of a pub game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock-keepers' suggests canal staff, but the locks are of hair. Skittles is a pub game like ninepin bowling.
explanation.definitionFit: Hairpins are U-shaped pins that hold locks of hair in place, so they keep the locks.

clue.text: Frank here is cover point

blocks.note: surface: a man named Frank is present; setter's reading: this is where a postmark franks the stamp
surface: the cricket fielding position; setter's reading: the item is a cover, the paper wrapper of a letter

explanation.surface: A cricket captain notes that a player called Frank is fielding at cover point.
explanation.walkthrough: Cover point is a fielding position on the off side in cricket. To frank a letter is to mark its postage, done on this paper cover.
explanation.definitionFit: An envelope is the paper cover enclosing a letter, and its corner is where the postage is franked.

clue.text: Moroccan fruit

blocks.note: first meaning: a native of Tangier, in Morocco
second meaning: the small loose-skinned orange

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one phrase about a fruit grown in Morocco, but the first word is a separate meaning: an inhabitant of Tangier.
explanation.definitionFit: The citrus fruit takes its name from Tangier, whose people are also called Tangerines.

clue.text: What tailors do now and then

definitions.note: cryptic: read as two words, FIT FULLY

blocks.note: first meaning, read cryptically: tailors fit a garment fully to the customer
second meaning: intermittently, in fits and starts

explanation.surface: A note on the occasional work habits of tailors.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a pun: split the answer into two words and it says what a tailor does to a suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitfully means irregularly or intermittently, happening only at intervals rather than continuously.

clue.text: South Pacific islands link up for mutual benefit

definitions.note: describes the society rather than naming it

blocks.note: two South Pacific archipelagos: the Friendly Islands (Tonga) and the Society Islands (Tahiti's group)

explanation.surface: Pacific island nations agree to cooperate for their shared advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: Both names come from the one phrase: Tonga was once called the Friendly Islands and Tahiti belongs to the Society Islands. A friendly society is a British mutual insurance club.
explanation.definitionFit: A friendly society is an association whose members pay in to insure one another against sickness and hardship, a mutual organisation.

clue.text: Where to find a tumulus in Cumbria

definitions.text: Where to find a tumulus in Cumbria

blocks.note: surface: an archaeological site; setter's reading: a tumulus is a barrow, so find the place a Barrow is in
the Cumbrian peninsula that gives the town Barrow its full name

explanation.surface: A guidebook question about locating an ancient burial mound in north-west England.
explanation.walkthrough: A tumulus is a barrow, and Barrow-in-Furness is a shipbuilding town in Cumbria, so the barrow is 'in' this district.
explanation.definitionFit: The town's full name Barrow-in-Furness literally places a barrow inside this Cumbrian peninsula.

clue.text: Painter left one road out

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or not in place, so the letters are disarranged

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An artist abandoned one route on his journey.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo da Vinci was the Italian Renaissance painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper.

clue.text: George, in the old number, gives conflicting replies

indicators.note: in places one name inside the words that follow it

blocks.note: ye is an archaic spelling of the
NO is the abbreviation for number
George Sand, the French novelist

explanation.surface: A man called George, singing an old tune, gives answers that contradict each other.
explanation.walkthrough: George Sand was the pen name of the French novelist Aurore Dupin; ye is the archaic 'the' of 'Ye Olde Tea Shoppe'.
explanation.definitionFit: Answering yes and no means giving two opposing replies at once, an equivocal response.

clue.text: John's Italian version of opera when put on first

definitions.text: of opera when put on first
definitions.note: cryptic: the word that names an opera once DON is put before it

blocks.note: first meaning: the Italian form of the name John

blocks.clueFragment: of opera when put on first
blocks.note: second meaning: put DON in front and you have Mozart's opera Don ...

explanation.surface: A programme note about an Italian production of an opera, with a singer called John.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half leaves the solver to supply DON, the title word that is 'put on first' to make Mozart's opera Don Giovanni.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni is the Italian equivalent of the English given name John, from the same Hebrew original.

clue.text: Clutches rail: do so when in trouble

indicators.note: words in trouble are in disorder, so their letters are jumbled

blocks.note: BR is British Rail, the old UK railway network
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice to grab the handrail when you are in difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clutches' looks like a verb about gripping, but it is the plural noun for batches of eggs. BR (British Rail) was the national railway of the UK.
explanation.definitionFit: A clutch is a set of eggs or chicks hatched together, and a brood is the same thing.

clue.text: Young rascal recognised as holder of US State record

indicators.note: a holder keeps something inside it, so one word goes around the others

blocks.note: recognised, noticed, observed
PA is the postal abbreviation for Pennsylvania
LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: A young tearaway turns out to hold a record in one American state.
explanation.walkthrough: The state and the record go in together as one pair. A spalpeen is an Irish word for a scamp or good-for-nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Spalpeen is an Irish term for a rascal or rogue, often used of a mischievous boy.

clue.text: Artist one put in the study

definitions.text: Artist one put in the study

indicators.note: to put something in a place is to place it inside, so the first parts go within the last

blocks.note: a den is a private study or workroom
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An artist is installed in the study to work.
explanation.walkthrough: The artist and the one go in together, after the first two letters of the study. The whole clue also defines the result: André Derain was a French painter.
explanation.definitionFit: André Derain was a French Fauvist painter, a leading figure alongside Matisse in early twentieth-century art.

clue.text: Fully anaesthetised, father has lesions cured (nothing removed)

indicators.note: nothing is the round letter zero, and removed tells us to take it out
curing changes the state of something, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: PA is an informal word for father
taken as written

explanation.surface: A patient father under full anaesthetic has his wounds treated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing' is the letter O, which looks like zero; take it out before rearranging what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fully anaesthetised feels no pain, so the procedure is painless for them.

clue.text: But Alonso did not really suffer this

definitions.text: But Alonso did not really suffer this

blocks.note: surface: some man named Alonso; setter's reading: the King of Naples in The Tempest, believed drowned
Ariel's song says the drowned father suffers a transformation under the waves, but Alonso is alive

explanation.surface: An oddly specific remark that one Alonso escaped some misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Tempest Ariel sings to Ferdinand that his father 'doth suffer a sea-change into something rich and strange', yet Alonso never drowned.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's phrase for the drowned man's transformation has become the idiom for any profound change.

clue.text: Sees composition to be classical

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so the letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone judges a piece of music to be in the classical style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classical' does not mean the music here but Latin, the classical language: the definition is the Latin verb 'to be'.
explanation.definitionFit: Esse is the Latin infinitive meaning 'to be', familiar from phrases such as in esse.

clue.text: Paper by thick-skinned brute

blocks.note: first meaning: a traditional large size of drawing paper
second meaning: the pachyderm, whose name means thick-skinned

explanation.surface: A newspaper article written by an insensitive bully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper' looks like a newspaper but is a standard sheet size, elephant, from the old British paper sizes.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephant is both an old paper size and the large thick-skinned animal, here called a brute as beasts are.

clue.text: He provides cavalry with means for a flanking attack

definitions.text: He provides cavalry with means for a flanking attack

blocks.note: surface: a quartermaster supplying mounted troops
setter's reading: the attack is on the horse's own flanks, which riders dig with spurs

explanation.surface: A military supplier equips horsemen to outflank the enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flanking attack' sounds tactical, but the flanks are the horse's sides, which a rider kicks with spurs.
explanation.definitionFit: A spurrier is a craftsman who makes spurs, the spiked heel pieces riders use to urge a horse on.

clue.text: Old bird in double act

blocks.note: act gives DO (to do is to act), and double means write it twice

explanation.surface: An elderly woman takes part in a comedy double act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old bird' can be slang for an elderly woman, but here it is literal: an extinct bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The dodo was a flightless bird of Mauritius, extinct since the late seventeenth century.

clue.text: It's rubbed off, I trusted, somehow

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the order of the letters is left open

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who was trusting finds their confidence has worn away.
explanation.definitionFit: Detritus is debris worn away from rock by erosion, literally material rubbed off a surface.

clue.text: School team relegated?

blocks.note: a relegated team goes down a division
a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: A school's sports team has been dropped to a lower league.
explanation.walkthrough: Downside is a Roman Catholic boarding school in Somerset, England, run by Benedictine monks.
explanation.definitionFit: Downside School is a well-known English independent school attached to Downside Abbey.

clue.text: Fellow-diner in trouble with drink

blocks.note: to be in a mess is to be in trouble
maté is a South American herbal tea

explanation.surface: A dinner companion has got into difficulties through drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: Maté (written MATE in the grid) is the caffeinated infusion drunk from a gourd in Argentina and Uruguay.
explanation.definitionFit: A messmate is someone who eats in the same mess, the shared dining room of a ship or barracks.

clue.text: Cornish location for Light Division

blocks.note: first meaning: ..., a village on the Lizard peninsula in Cornwall
second meaning: the upright bar dividing the lights, or panes, of a window

explanation.surface: A base in Cornwall for an army regiment, the Light Division.
explanation.walkthrough: The Light Division is a real British infantry formation, but here light means a window pane.
explanation.definitionFit: A mullion is the vertical stone or wooden bar that separates the lights of a window.

clue.text: This flighty, emperor born in this?

definitions.text: This flighty, emperor born in this?

blocks.note: surface: a fickle emperor; setter's reading
an emperor's child is said to be born in this colour, the colour of imperial rank

explanation.surface: A riddle about a capricious ruler and the circumstances of his birth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flighty' is not fickle but literally able to fly: the purple emperor is a British butterfly. To be 'born in the purple' is to be born into royalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Purple is the colour linked with emperors since Rome, giving both the butterfly's name and the idiom for royal birth.

clue.text: Joined together the . company he split

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
taken as written
rent is an old past tense of rend, meaning torn or split

explanation.surface: A man broke up the business that had once been united.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray full stop is a printing blemish in the newspaper copy. 'Split' looks like an action, but it is the old past participle rent.
explanation.definitionFit: Coherent means sticking together as a unified whole, from the Latin cohaerere, to cling together.

clue.text: Defences of cats such as Macavity

definitions.text: Defences of cats such as Macavity

blocks.note: surface: claws and teeth, the way a cat protects itself
setter's reading: Macavity, T. S. Eliot's Mystery Cat, defends himself with excuses, always having one ready

explanation.surface: How cats protect themselves, with a famous fictional feline as example.
explanation.walkthrough: In Eliot's Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats, Macavity the criminal cat 'always has an alibi, and one or two to spare'.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a defence showing the accused was elsewhere when the crime happened, Macavity's stock in trade.

clue.text: Scientist given one in Germany by Gertrude

blocks.note: ein is German for one
Gertrude Stein, the American writer

explanation.surface: A scientist in Germany receives something from a woman called Gertrude.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Einstein was the physicist behind relativity, the archetypal scientist of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Mournful commentary on the dry spell

indicators.note: a spell is a magic charm that transforms things, so the letters before it change shape

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gloomy commentator laments a long drought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry spell' reads as one phrase, but 'spell' is split off to act on the three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A threnody is a song or poem of lamentation for the dead, a formal expression of grief.

clue.text: Interminable oriental feast

indicators.note: something interminable has no end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: oriental means from the East

explanation.surface: A banquet in the Far East that seems to go on for ever.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter is the principal Christian feast, celebrating the resurrection, so it is a feast in the church calendar.
